# JOURNAL — optimizer handover (append-only, whole run)

YOU (the optimizer) own this file. It is the running, accumulating handover across ALL iterations — accepted AND rejected — and it is NEVER reset. Each iteration you APPEND one new entry at the bottom (under the marker line); you do NOT edit or delete earlier entries. Read the whole journal before proposing, so you build on EVERY prior attempt (not just the last accepted one) and never re-test a refuted idea.

You CANNOT know your own gate result while you write — the harness scores you AFTER you stop and stamps a **RESULT** line (outcome + Δ + the tasks you measurably broke/fixed, plus the ones whose move was too small to resolve) right below your entry. So do NOT write 'what worked' as a guess. To learn what actually worked, READ the framework RESULT lines of prior entries (and LEDGER.md): an entry whose RESULT says `rejected` with `broke={...}` tells you which specific edits to drop or redesign — its diff.patch is in ./prior_iterations/<id>/.

Append your entry for THIS iteration below the marker, using this shape (INTENT only — the framework appends the RESULT):

    ## Iteration <your candidate id> — <one-line headline of what you tried>
    - Changes I made (1 line per edit; name the file/tool + cluster it targets):
    - Per change, the EXPECTED effect + why it's safe (which failing task it should fix;
      why no passing task changes behavior):
    - Building on prior RESULTS: which prior entries' broke/fixed I used, and what I
      did NOT re-try because a prior RESULT showed it regressed (cite ids):
    - Refuted hypotheses (a prior RESULT proved this is NOT the fix — never re-test):
    - High-value clusters still NOT cracked (and the guard/tool designs already tried):
    - Plateau signal (are the last few RESULTs flat/negative? if so, which LEVER to switch
      to — e.g. a NEW composite tool instead of another guard, or prompt instead of code):
    - Focus next iteration:

## Iteration cand_0001 — empty seed: created prompt.md + task_template.md around one root cause (formula written instead of value) plus a required verification round

- Changes I made (1 line per edit; file + cluster):
  - E1 `prompt.md` §"How your work is graded" — the output contract: the grader reads
    `data_only=True` and never recalculates, so every graded cell must hold a literal value;
    wrong/right code pair. Cluster 1 (formula-as-answer, 25 of 26 failures).
  - E2 `task_template.md` §"How to work" — ordered 4-step procedure (inspect → compute+write
    → verify → fix), and DELETED the built-in line "once that file exists, you are done".
    Cluster 2 (no verification; 9 traces one-shot in 4 turns).
  - E3 `prompt.md` §"The grader's value comparison, exactly" — the `transform_value` /
    `compare_cell_value` table (type mismatch fails; numbers round to 2dp; numeric strings
    coerce; datetime → serial rounded to a whole day; `None`==`""`). Cluster 3/5 (type
    infidelity, Excel-error text).
  - E4 `prompt.md` §"Change only what was asked" + template checklist item 3 — every cell of
    `answer_position` is compared and untouched cells must keep their original input value.
    Cluster 4 (wrote past the answer / overwrote originals).
  - E5 `prompt.md` §"Role" — resolves the conflict that made E1 look like disobedience:
    "suggest a formula" describes the RESULT; the deliverable is the computed value.
  - E6 `prompt.md` §"Writing the literal value" — Excel→Python translation list
    («redacted»…) and the openpyxl
    cached-value hazard for pre-existing formulas inside the answer range.
  - E7 `prompt.md` §"Check your logic against the examples you were given" + template
    checklist item 4 — values already in the answer range ("as I have manually done in
    column B", a header "Expected Result") are ground truth, not cells to overwrite.
  - E8 `prompt.md` §"`answer_position` and sheets" + template field descriptions —
    range/sheet resolution, Cell- vs Sheet-Level semantics, preview is lossy, formatting is
    not graded.
- Per change, EXPECTED effect + why it's safe: E1 is the big one — 15 failing tasks have
  `test_case_results=[1]` with `test_case_results_no_recalc=[0]`, i.e. correct logic and a
  wrong artifact, so they should flip on the contract alone; E2 should catch the rest
  independently (I ran the verify snippet against a reconstruction of 37378's real output
  and the assertion fires). Safety: all 14 passing tasks already compute literals in Python
  (zero write a formula; 31628 comments "# Write the static number, not a formula"), so E1
  and E3–E7 only state what passing behaviour already satisfies. E2 is the only edit that
  changes passing *trajectories*; it is bounded because the graded submission is the last
  code block that WROTE the file (`_artifact_stamp`/`solution_code`), so a read-only verify
  round cannot replace a correct answer, and `MAX_TURNS=30` with passing tasks already at
  4–13 rounds. I deliberately did NOT write "every answer cell must be non-empty" in the
  checklist — that would false-alarm on 382-10 / 227-40 / 402-43 / 142-12, which correctly
  leave cells blank.
- Building on prior RESULTS: none — first iteration, LEDGER/RUNMAP/rejected.jsonl all empty.
  Nothing re-tried, nothing avoided on prior evidence.
- Refuted hypotheses: none established yet. Worth recording what is NOT the problem:
  this is not an environment fault — all 26 failing traces executed cleanly and produced an
  output file; and it is not a "the agent can't do the task" gap — 15 failures had correct
  logic.
- High-value clusters still NOT cracked: 51-12 (VBA restart semantics, answer came out a
  number too low) and 43436 (month-boundary counting, 5 of 15 cells too high) are genuine
  one-off logic errors; no general prose rule reaches them without encoding the answer, so I
  left them. Also unproven: whether the required verify round actually gets USED or gets
  skipped like any other instruction — if the next RESULT shows cluster 1 fixed but
  clusters 4/6 untouched, the verify round is being narrated and not run, and the lever to
  switch to is making the checklist output something the agent must quote.
- Plateau signal: n/a, first iteration from an empty seed.
- Focus next iteration: read the RESULT per task. If cluster 1 flipped (expect the ~15
  logic-was-right tasks), the remaining failures are logic/type/scope and the next lever is
  a worked example per *residual* mismatch class in the feedback (`num_high`/`num_low`,
  `type_other`, `kept`), not more contract text. Do not grow `prompt.md` further without a
  measured reason — prune instead.

> **RESULT (framework, measured):** ACCEPTED (new champion) · val=0.925 Δ=+0.575 · fixed={12864, 267-18, 2768, 37378, 37456, 39046, 45635, 46897, 48588, 48620, 48921, 50768, 51-12, 53383, 53647, 54144, 55049, 55979, 56563, 59196, 7902, 8942, 9569, 9726} · broke={402-43} · unresolved={—} (moved less than 2·SE of its own measurement — NOT evidence the edit touched those tasks; do not redesign on them).
<!-- cand_0001: ACCEPTED val=0.925 Δ=+0.575 -->

## Iteration cand_0002 — two of the three residual failures are collateral damage from cand_0001's own "pre-filled cells are ground truth" rule; narrowed it with a discriminating condition instead of adding rules, plus a snapshot-vs-overlap counting section and a don't-replace-your-own-good-answer guard

- Changes I made (1 line per edit; name the file/tool + cluster it targets):
  - E1 `prompt.md` §"Check your logic against the examples you were given" (rewrite) — dropped
    cand_0001's absolute "a rule that disagrees with a stated example is wrong no matter how
    reasonable it looks"; replaced with a two-branch test (a disagreement a *different rule*
    explains → the rule is wrong; a disagreement **no** rule explains, where the real source
    data holds a value and the user's hand-typed illustration is blank → **source data wins**),
    plus "an example corrects your RULE, it never becomes your ANSWER" and a shrinking-answer
    guard. Cluster 1 / `402-43`.
  - E2 `prompt.md` §"Change only what was asked" (replace the "ground truth" bullet) — never
    gate the write on `if cell.value is None`; compute your rule's value for every cell the
    instruction asks about *including pre-filled ones*, then branch: agree → leave; differ and
    the existing value is the kind your rule produces → your rule is wrong (minus four named
    benign causes); differ and it is a conventional stand-in (`n/a`, `-`, `?`, `TBD`, `""`, a
    leftover `#VALUE!`/`#NUM!`) → it is a placeholder, **write over it**. Plus an explicit
    not-covered list and "keep their input VALUE" (a formula left in place still scores 0).
    Cluster 1 / `59595`.
  - E3 `prompt.md` new §"Counting things that are open 'as of' a date vs 'during' a period" —
    both rules as two lines of Python, overlap ≥ snapshot so misusing overlap makes a column
    uniformly too high, a label naming one moment is a snapshot even when the prose describes a
    window, plus two data-side identities to check against. Cluster 2 / `43436`.
  - E4 `task_template.md` step-1 close + checklist item 4 — step 1 must end with an explicit
    EXAMPLE/PLACEHOLDER-tagged list of every worked value available; item 4 becomes "run it,
    don't assert it": print one `worked value → my rule's value` pair per line and report the
    item by quoting them. A disagreement means **investigate**, with the four benign causes
    enumerated. Cluster 2, and the mechanism that makes E1–E2 bite.
  - E5 `task_template.md` step-3 snippet + checklist item 2 — added a `Counter` type tally over
    the graded range; item 2 now requires that no cell you were asked to fill still holds a
    carried-over placeholder, scoped to "the data cells your own rule fills" with int+float,
    `None`, and header-str mixes explicitly blessed. Cluster 1 / `59595`.
  - E6 `task_template.md` step 4 — the graded submission is the **last** code block that wrote
    `output_path`, so a later write replaces the earlier wholesale; name the wrong cells before
    rewriting, and a rewrite that fills fewer answer cells is evidence the rewrite is the
    mistake. Cluster 1 / `402-43`.
- Per change, the EXPECTED effect + why it's safe (which failing task it should fix; why no
  passing task changes behavior):
  - E1 → `402-43`. Its turn 6 wrote a correct 114-cell answer; turn 7 printed its only
    disagreement as three cells where the hand-typed demo block is blank but the real header
    row holds `'Col5'/'Col6'/'Col7'`; turn 10 transcribed the demo block, dropping to 111, and
    the grader says "111 of 330 … 3 cell(s) are empty where a value is expected". That is
    exactly branch 2, so the agent keeps its computed value. Safe: the edit only changes what
    happens *after* a disagreement, and only in the no-rule-explains sub-case; it strengthens
    the "your rule is wrong" branch that `37378`/`39046`/`48527`/`54144` rely on. No passing
    trace transcribes a demo block, and `227-40` actively needs the source-data-wins clause.
  - E2 → `59595`. Turn 1 printed `C4 raw: 'n/a' str`; turn 2 gated on `is None` under the
    comment "Preserve user-provided/example values" while its own output already held the right
    answers (`C4 total=4`, `C5 total=6`, `C6 total=12`); grader says "3 cell(s) hold str where
    int was expected", and two 1.0-scoring sibling rollouts write exactly 4/6/12. Safe because
    the census says so, not because it feels narrow: 24 of 37 passing tasks have pre-filled
    cells inside `answer_position`, and I classified all of them — headers/labels and
    input-columns-inside-the-range are covered by the not-covered bullet; 16 tasks hit the
    "they agree" branch unchanged; `55049`/`56563` already overwrite `#VALUE!`/`#NUM!`
    placeholders *today*, which cand_0001's "leave untouched" wording contradicted, so this
    edit also resolves a live conflict in the parent prompt. **Zero** passing tasks are in the
    dangerous category (a different-rule pre-filled cell this edit would overwrite). The one
    trap the census caught: `80-42` holds literal `'N/A'`/`'None'` as real source data, so the
    discriminator decides by **re-derivation, not characters** — if your rule produces `N/A`,
    the cell agrees and you leave it.
  - E3 → `43436`. Its turn 2 implemented overlap. I recomputed both rules from the workbook XML:
    they differ in exactly 5 of 15 cells with the agent higher in all 5, matching "5 of 15
    cell(s) differ … 5 cell(s) hold a number HIGHER than expected" uniquely (the rival
    "ignore the close date" rule differs in 9 cells). The headers the agent printed itself are
    snapshot labels ("Open by end of Jul 2022") while the prose paraphrase describes overlap.
    Safe: I grepped all 37 passing instructions for as-of/by-end-of/still-open/outstanding/
    aging/backlog language — the only hit is `2768`, which is inventory allocation with no date
    window and no open/closed counting. The section supplies both rules rather than mandating
    one, so its blast radius is effectively empty.
  - E4/E5/E6 add output and preconditions, not values. Round budget checked: `MAX_TURNS=30`,
    `VERIFY_TURNS=3` non-writing rounds after the first write, inspection rounds before the
    first write are free; 28 passing tasks finish in 4 assistant turns and 8 in 5, so I folded
    every new print into the **existing** step-3 script in the same round rather than adding a
    round. E6's precondition is only reachable after a correct write already exists, and 35 of
    37 passing tasks write once and never revisit.
- Building on prior RESULTS: cand_0001 ACCEPTED, `fixed={24 tasks}`, **`broke={402-43}`** — that
  one word is the whole iteration. I read its diff.patch, found `402-43` was passing on the seed
  by computing the header from row 1 and never consulting the demo block, and traced the
  regression to its E7 ("values already present are ground truth") + the absolute example clause
  in its "check your logic" section. `59595` fails by the identical mechanism. So I did NOT add a
  seventh rule on top; I narrowed the two existing ones with discriminating conditions (skill
  levers 9 + 4) and left the formula/type/scope contract from cand_0001 E1/E3/E4/E6/E8 untouched,
  since it is what the 24 fixed tasks depend on. I also did not re-try the thing cand_0001's own
  JOURNAL warned about — "do not grow prompt.md without a measured reason, prune instead" — in
  the form of blind pruning: 37 of 40 tasks pass, so I had no evidence any section is unused, and
  deleting what I cannot show is dead is the edit the skill warns against. Two of six edits
  replace existing text rather than appending.
- Refuted hypotheses (a prior RESULT proved this is NOT the fix — never re-test):
  - **"Pre-filled values in the answer range are always ground truth; leave them untouched."**
    cand_0001's RESULT (`broke={402-43}`) is the proof. Stated absolutely it costs more tasks
    than it wins — `59595` loses three cells to an `'n/a'` it refused to overwrite, and `402-43`
    threw away a correct 114-cell answer for a hand-typed illustration. The rule is only safe
    with the stand-in-vs-worked-value discriminator attached.
  - **"A rule that disagrees with a stated example is wrong no matter how reasonable it looks."**
    Same RESULT. An incomplete illustration is not a rule.
  - Not refuted but worth not re-deriving: no environment faults exist in this split. All three
    failures have `test_case_results == test_case_results_no_recalc == [0]`, i.e. wrong values,
    not formula-vs-value artifacts; every trace ran cleanly and produced a graded output file.
    There is also no flakiness and no partial credit anywhere — one trial per task, every
    passing task exactly 1.0 — so the entire recoverable budget this iteration is 3 tasks
    = 0.075 and the dominant risk is regression, not timidity.
- High-value clusters still NOT cracked (and the guard/tool designs already tried):
  - **Prose-vs-header conflicts in general.** `43436`'s gold follows the column headers against
    the instruction's prose paraphrase, and a global "the header wins" precedence rule is the
    obvious generalisation. I deliberately skipped it: it is an UNBOUNDED decision-rule edit and
    I could not enumerate the passing tasks in that class to prove none has gold following the
    prose — the audit found `59196` sitting one pre-filled cell away from flipping (prose
    "return the heading of that column" → `'D'`, vs header `H2='MAX'`). A future iteration that
    wants this needs the prose/header conflict census first. E3 covers the verified case with a
    narrow condition instead.
  - **Whether the forced rule-check in E4 is actually run or just narrated.** cand_0001 asked
    the open version of this question; all three failing traces answered it badly, emitting
    `4. … : checked` lines that merely restate their own rule (`43436`: "Counts use the stated
    rule … checked"; `59595`: invented an exemption the instruction never states). E4's
    quote-the-printed-pairs contract is my attempt; it is untested.
- Plateau signal (are the last few RESULTs flat/negative? if so, which LEVER to switch to):
  no plateau — one RESULT so far and it was +0.575. But the headroom collapsed: 0.075 total
  remains, and a single speculative edit that breaks one passing task costs 0.025, so from here
  the search is regression-bound rather than idea-bound. The lever that follows is **audit
  before ship, not after**: see META_INSIGHTS: the blast-radius audit changed four of my six
  edits and caught a ~10-task regression in my own draft of E4.
- Focus next iteration: read the per-task RESULT and treat it as the experiment it is. If
  `402-43` + `59595` flip, cluster 1 is closed and the only residual is `43436`-class logic —
  at which point the remaining lever is the prose/header census above, or accepting 0.975 and
  spending the iteration on *robustness* (the 8 passing tasks that finish with zero spare verify
  rounds are the flakiness risk nobody has measured). If they do NOT flip, the discriminator was
  read and not applied, and the lever must become structural: make the agent print the
  `existing value → my rule's value → decision` triple for every pre-filled answer cell, the way
  E4 forces the worked-value pairs, rather than stating the condition in prose a third time. If
  the RESULT shows a *regression* on a passing task, check it against the four benign
  disagreement causes in E4 first — that is where my edits are closest to the line.

> **RESULT (framework, measured):** REJECTED (champion unchanged) · val=0.900 Δ=-0.025 · fixed={59595} · broke={50768, 80-42} · unresolved={—} (moved less than 2·SE of its own measurement — NOT evidence the edit touched those tasks; do not redesign on them). — its WHOLE batch was reverted; re-introduce only the edits that did NOT break a task above, dropping/redesigning the ones that did.
<!-- cand_0002: rejected val=0.900 Δ=-0.025 -->

## Iteration cand_0003 — re-attacked all three residual failures from cand_0001 (cand_0002's whole batch was reverted), but first pinned WHY cand_0002 broke `80-42` and `50768` and designed those two mechanisms out: no stand-in character list, no anti-`is None` rule, no anti-shrink guard, no two-rule menu

- Changes I made (1 line per edit; name the file/tool + cluster it targets):
  - E1 `prompt.md` §"Change only what was asked" (new bullet AFTER cand_0001's unchanged
    "ground truth" bullet) — **the one type-conflict exception**: compute your rule's value for
    every cell the instruction asks about (pre-filled or not, "so that an already-populated cell
    is a comparison you make rather than a cell you silently skip"), and overwrite on **exactly
    one combination** — your rule yields a number or a date *and* the cell holds text that does

# INSIGHTS — summarized, verified findings (accumulate across the whole run)

The JOURNAL is your per-iteration diary; THIS file is the distilled, VERIFIED takeaway a future iteration should read instead of re-reading the whole journal or old sessions/traces. Update it whenever you have a genuinely NEW, confirmed finding (an accepted/rejected RESULT counts as confirmation; a guess does not) — not every iteration needs a new entry. Structure each addition as:

    ## <task or mechanism name>
    - What worked (confirmed by a RESULT, cite the candidate id):
    - What didn't (confirmed by a RESULT, cite the candidate id):
    - Promising but not yet tried:

## The grading contract (verified from the scorer source + an openpyxl experiment, not from a RESULT)
- What worked (confirmed by a RESULT): nothing yet — cand_0001 is the first candidate.
- MECHANISM, independently verified and safe for any future iteration to rely on:
  - Primary metric is `hard_no_recalc`. `compare_workbooks` in
    `third_party/spreadsheetbench/evaluation/evaluation.py` opens both files with
    `openpyxl.load_workbook(..., data_only=True)`; `adapter._recalc_workbook` is NOT applied
    for this metric. **A formula written with openpyxl therefore reads back as `None`** —
    tested directly on openpyxl 3.1.5. On the seed, 25 of 26 failures wrote formulas, and 15
    of them had `test_case_results=[1]` / `test_case_results_no_recalc=[0]`: correct logic,
    wrong artifact. This is the single largest lever in this benchmark.
  - `compare_cell_value` fails on `type(v1) != type(v2)` AFTER `transform_value`: numbers →
    `round(float(v),2)`; a numeric *string* → the same (so `"3"` == `3`); non-numeric strings
    compared exactly; `datetime` → Excel serial **rounded to a whole day** (so a time
    component ≥ 12:00 shifts the date by one day); `time` → `"HH:MM:SS"`; `None` == `""`.
    A `datetime.date` assigned via openpyxl reads back as `datetime.datetime` (tested).
  - `cell_level_compare` compares EVERY cell of `answer_position`, and the gold is the input
    workbook with the answer added — so cells the instruction does not ask about must keep
    their original input value. An unprefixed range is graded on `wb_gt.sheetnames[0]`.
  - Verification is structurally cheap: `solution_code` is the last code block that CHANGED
    the output file (`adapter._artifact_stamp`), so read-only rounds cannot replace a correct
    submission. `MAX_TURNS=30`, `VERIFY_TURNS=3`, and inspection rounds *before* the first
    write are not counted against `VERIFY_TURNS`.
  - Fill- and font-colour comparison is commented out in the vendored scorer: **formatting is
    not graded.** Effort spent on `PatternFill`/`number_format` is wasted.
- What didn't (confirmed by a RESULT): nothing yet.
- Promising but not yet tried: a per-mismatch-class worked example keyed to the feedback's own
  taxonomy (`num_high`/`num_low`, `type_other`, `kept`, `extra`) once the formula cluster is
  out of the way and those classes are what remains.

## Pre-filled cells inside `answer_position` — the "ground truth" rule is only safe with a discriminator
- What worked (confirmed by a RESULT, cite the candidate id): cand_0001's rule caught real cases —
  24 of its 40 tasks flipped and several of them (`37378`, `39046`, `48527`, `48588`, `54144`,
  `9569`) do have worked leading rows the agent must reproduce rather than overwrite.
- What didn't (confirmed by a RESULT, cand_0001, `broke={402-43}`): stating it **absolutely**
  ("treat values already present as ground truth, leave them untouched" + "a rule that disagrees
  with a stated example is wrong no matter how reasonable it looks") costs tasks. `402-43`
  regressed from the seed: it computed a correct 114-cell answer, found 3 cells where the user's
  hand-typed demonstration block is blank but the real header row holds values, and transcribed
  the block over its own answer (111 cells, grader: "3 cell(s) are empty where a value is
  expected"). `59595` fails identically with an `'n/a'` it refused to overwrite while its own
  output already held the right numbers. The wording also directly contradicted the behaviour of
  two tasks that pass *by overwriting*: `55049` (B3:B23 all `#VALUE!`) and `56563` (C14 `#NUM!`).
- MECHANISM, independently verified (census over all 37 passing tasks' input workbooks ∩ their
  `answer_position`, `/tmp/prefill_audit.py` — safe to rely on):
  - **24 of 37 passing tasks have pre-filled cells inside `answer_position`.** They fall into
    four benign categories: headers/labels inside the range (`382-10`, `142-12`, `463-17`,
    `560-12`, `395-36`), input columns sitting inside the graded range (`7902` D3:G6), worked
    leading rows the correct rule reproduces (16 tasks), and already-overwritten placeholders
    (`55049`, `56563`). **The dangerous fifth category — a pre-filled answer cell produced by a
    *different* rule that must be preserved — is EMPTY in this split.**
  - Only `47798` and `53383` gate a write on emptiness, and both would write byte-identical
    values either way, so removing the `is None` gate is behaviourally free on the passing set.
  - **Decide "placeholder" by re-derivation, not by characters.** `80-42`
    (`'Consolidate_ALL'!A2:L8000`, 47 975 pre-filled cells) holds `J2='N/A'` and `D2/E2/F2='None'`
    as *real gold data* copied from source sheets. A closed character list containing `N/A` would
    have told the agent to overwrite them. The safe formulation: if your rule, run over the source
    data, *produces* that text, the cell agrees and you leave it.
- Promising but not yet tried: forcing the agent to print the
  `existing value → my rule's value → decision` triple for every pre-filled answer cell, instead
  of stating the discriminating condition in prose.

## Worked values are weak evidence — four benign disagreements dominate
- What worked / what didn't: not yet confirmed by a RESULT; this is a census finding from
  cand_0002's blast-radius audit over the 37 passing traces, and it is the reason cand_0002's
  rule check says "investigate" rather than "fix the rule".
- MECHANISM: an instruction to fix the rule whenever a worked value disagrees would break ~10
  currently-passing tasks, because the disagreement is benign in four recurring ways:
  **hand-rounding** (`9569`: pre-filled `AO9=0.1707`, correct value `0.170687841` — and that
  task's own equality assert already fired once and cost it a round); **float-representation
  noise** (`54144`: `106.53999999999999` vs `106.54`); **a stale or broken formula cache** in the
  worked cell (`6698`, `48620`, `55049`, `56563` hold `#VALUE!`/`#NUM!`/older-data values); and
  **a neighbouring cell computed by a different rule** (`8942`, `37456`, `267-18` — read the
  worked cell's own header before believing it). The comparison must be done the way the grader
  does it (both sides rounded to 2 dp, numeric strings coerced), never with `==`.
- The one place a worked cell IS authoritative: **the exact spelling, case and spacing of text
  output.** A non-numeric string is compared character for character, so the sheet's own wording
  beats the instruction's paraphrase of it — `53383` turns on prose "matched" vs sheet `'Matched'`.

## Snapshot vs overlap counting (`43436`) — the gold rule is recoverable from the error signature
- What worked / didn't: not yet confirmed by a RESULT.
- MECHANISM, independently verified by recomputing both rules from the raw workbook XML: the agent
  used **interval overlap** (`created <= T2 and (closed is None or closed >= T1)`) where the gold
  wants an end-of-period **snapshot** (`created <= T and (closed is None or closed > T)`; closed
  *on* T counts as closed). Overlap counts a superset of snapshot, so the column comes out
  uniformly too high. The two rules differ in **exactly the 5 of 15 cells the grader names, with
  the agent higher in all 5**, which pins the rule uniquely — a rival hypothesis ("ignore the
  close date") differs in 9 cells and is excluded. The discriminator in the data: the column
  *headers* are snapshot labels ("Open by end of Jul 2022") while the instruction's prose
  paraphrase ("not closed before the first day of the month") describes overlap, **and the gold
  follows the headers**. Two identities catch the error without knowing the answer: a snapshot
  taken after the last closure in the sheet must equal the never-closed count; and a series of
  snapshots at increasing dates can only lose a record once its close date has passed.
- Promising but not yet tried: the general rule "a column header beats the instruction's prose".
  Deliberately NOT shipped in cand_0002 — it is unbounded, and the audit found `59196` one
  pre-filled cell away from flipping on it (prose "return the heading of that column" → `'D'` vs
  header `H2='MAX'`). It needs a prose/header conflict census across all 40 tasks first.

## Split characteristics worth not re-deriving
- One trial per task; **no partial credit and no flakiness anywhere** in this split — every
  passing task scores exactly 1.0, so each task is worth 0.025 and the val number is a plain
  pass count over 40.
- Round budget on the passing set: **28 tasks finish in 4 assistant turns, 8 in 5** — i.e. 8 tasks
  use all 3 `VERIFY_TURNS` with zero spare. An edit that adds a verification *round* (rather than
  more printing inside the existing round) is a silent regression risk on those 8.
- No environment faults exist in this split as of cand_0002: all failing traces execute cleanly,
  produce an output file, and are graded, with
  `test_case_results == test_case_results_no_recalc`.

## Confirmed by cand_0002's REJECT (val 0.900, broke={80-42, 50768}) — read before touching the "pre-filled cells" rule again

- **`80-42` broke for two independent reasons, both worth knowing in general.**
  (1) Its solution's *only* decision is an emptiness scan:
  `for r in range(2, 8001): if all(dest.cell(r,c).value is None for c in range(1,13)): first_blank = r`
  → `First blank destination row: 4000`, then it appends rows 4000–7997 below 3 998 pre-existing
  rows (`unchanged original mismatches: 0`). **Testing a cell for emptiness is the correct and
  only way to locate an append point** — a blanket "never decide what to write from
  `cell.value is None`" forbids the step the task *is*.
  (2) The task has **47 975 pre-filled cells inside `answer_position`**, including 3 998
  `J*='N/A'` and thousands of literal `'None'` strings, all **gold**. Any instruction phrased as
  a list of placeholder tokens is, on this task, an instruction to overwrite ~8 000 correct cells.
  Corollary already in this file, now measured: decide "placeholder" by **re-derivation and type
  conflict**, never by the characters.
  (3) It is also the context bomb: any "one line per pre-filled answer cell" verification prints
  47 975 lines. Cap every per-cell print, and scope worked-value comparisons to *the pre-filled
  cells your rule covers* (empty here) rather than to the range.
- **`50768` broke because its correct answer is mostly empty and partly string-typed.** Gold is
  **6 of 9 cells empty** (`F12:H14`); its own verify line is `graded non-empty: 3 of 9`, and the
  three filled cells are strings — `'4, 6'`, `'1, 3, 5'`, and `'2'` (a single ID **as a str**).
  So: an anti-shrink / "filling fewer answer cells is evidence the rewrite is the mistake" guard
  converts a correct answer into a bug signature, and any framing that treats "a non-numeric
  string sitting among numbers" as suspicious points straight at gold. **An empty answer cell and
  a string-typed numeric answer are both normal in this benchmark.** Its in-range `F14='1, 3, 5'`
  is additionally the *only* evidence fixing the matrix orientation, so weakening "a stated
  example is authoritative" costs this task as well.
- **A rule gated on a classification cannot repair a misclassification.** cand_0002 presented
  snapshot-vs-overlap as a menu plus sanity identities that only applied *after* the column had
  been classified; `43436` had already classified it wrongly, and the section did nothing (the
  task is not in cand_0002's `fixed`). When a failure is a wrong choice between two readings,
  **prescribe the answer** and supply falsification identities that hold **ungated**, computable
  from the data without knowing which reading is right.
- **Verified vacuous, do not re-derive:** the sibling-column falsification test on `43436`.
  `H1='Open as of today'` is a single instant, and the span rule over a zero-width window
  collapses to the moment rule — both readings reproduce `H2:H6 = 1,2,1,0,1`. A pre-filled
  sibling column only discriminates when its own reference window has non-zero width.
- **A cached formula value can be a *number* under an instruction that says to change it.**
  `6698`'s `G4` holds `'=SUM(COUNTIFS(...'` whose cached value is a stale number, and the task is
  "**Modify** my formula … to also include an additional condition"; `48620`'s `E2:E7` is the
  text analogue (`ws[f"E{r}"] = ws[f"B{r}"].value`). So any rule of the form "the existing value
  is the same *kind* as your rule's output → leave the cell alone" regresses these. The safe
  shape is a pure *permission to overwrite* under a narrow condition, adding no new instruction
  to leave anything.

## The prompt shipped code that crashes on a whole input shape (single-cell `answer_position`)

- What worked (confirmed by a RESULT): not yet — shipped in cand_0004, whose gate outcome cannot
  be positive (see the next section). The *diagnosis*, however, is as hard as evidence gets here.
- MECHANISM, verified from all 40 traces of cand_0003 — safe to rely on:
  - `ws["B7"]` returns a bare `Cell`; only `ws["B7:B7"]` and `ws["C3:C6"]` return a tuple of row
    tuples. So `[c.coordinate for row in ws[rng] for c in row]` — the line cand_0001/cand_0003
    shipped inside the **mandated** step-3 snippet — raises
    `TypeError: 'Cell' object is not iterable` whenever `answer_position` names one cell.
  - **The correlation is perfect in both directions.** Single-cell `answer_position` in this
    split: `{31628 B1, 46897 I3, 51-12 B6, 55979 'Calc'!B7, 56563 C14, 8942 'Overview'!B5,
    9726 J2}` = 7 of 40 (17.5%). Tasks with ≥1 traceback: the identical 7, one traceback each.
    Single-cell without a crash: none. Crash without single-cell: none. The other 33 finish in
    4 assistant turns with zero exceptions. It is deterministic, not flaky.
  - Cost per affected task: one round, and ~8–10k tokens (4 of the 7 are among the 8 most
    expensive runs). Because `verify_left -= 1` fires on any round that leaves the output file's
    stamp unchanged, **each of the 7 spends one of its three `VERIFY_TURNS` on the prompt's own
    bug** — the verify round is a second-try safety net there, not a first-try one. `51-12`
    (6 assistant turns, 5 code blocks) is the deepest consumption in the split.
  - **Patching the snippet fixes only 5 of the 7.** `46897` r1 and `9726` r1 crash in the agent's
    *own* exploration code (`for row in ws[ANSWER_RANGE]:`), before step 3 exists — the idiom is a
    model habit as well as a template defect, so the fact must also be stated as a rule in
    `prompt.md`. `range_boundaries` appeared **nowhere** in `prompt.md`, `task_template.md` or
    `guidance/` before cand_0004: a genuine knowledge gap, not a skipped rule.
  - **The fix is the agent's own convergent repair.** Both recovery rounds I diffed are
    byte-for-byte re-runs of the crashed block with only the enumeration swapped, and the full
    checklist survives (nothing degrades to a narrower check):
    `min_col, min_row, max_col, max_row = range_boundaries(RNG)` then a nested
    `range()` loop. `8942` imports from `openpyxl.utils`, `55979` from `openpyxl.utils.cell` —
    both available in the sandbox, which is the empirical proof the import path is safe.
  - **Equivalence proof for the safe-edit test:** a `coords()` helper built on
    `range_boundaries` + `get_column_letter` returns a list element-identical and in the same
    reading order to the old comprehension on **every** multi-cell range in the split, so
    replacing the line cannot change the 33 unaffected tasks. It additionally handles the
    comma-separated multi-part `answer_position` the prompt's own spec allows (none occurs in
    val), the malformed prefix `worksheet2'!C3:C6` (`53383` — **the benchmark's quoting is not
    always balanced**; strip `'` off both ends, never slice `[1:-1]`), and the CJK sheet name
    `'工作表1'` (`560-12`).
- Promising but not yet tried: nothing further on this cluster — it is closed.

## The round budget the agent is told about is not the one that binds

- MECHANISM, read off the adapter's loop (independently verified, safe to rely on):
  `MAX_TURNS=30` (what the template's "You have up to {max_turns} rounds" renders to) **never
  binds** — the deepest run in the split is 6 assistant turns. What binds is
  `VERIFY_TURNS=3`: any round leaving the output file's stamp unchanged does `verify_left -= 1`,
  and `verify_left <= 0` ends the episode. A round that **raises** therefore spends a third of the
  verification budget while returning no information about the answer. A round that *does* rewrite
  `output_path` costs nothing from that budget — **deliberately not stated in the prompt**, since
  it is an invitation to burn rounds on gratuitous rewrites.
  The template's old line "verifying costs you nothing but a round" was the only factually wrong
  sentence in the capability; its true half (a non-writing round cannot replace a correct
  submission) is what makes the agent willing to verify at all and must be kept.
- Also measured over all 40: **zero `AssertionError`** — no `assert` in the agent's own
  verification code fired anywhere; **zero `except: pass`** in agent code, so the 7 tracebacks are
  the complete failure inventory rather than a sample; and no harness limit-notice text exists in
  any trace. Context cost is entirely a **round-1** phenomenon: `80-42` prints 33 186 chars /
  210 lines in round 1 while no verify-round output anywhere exceeds 7.2k. Step 3 caps its own
  printing; step 1 had no analogue until cand_0004.

## The eight `agree? False` overrides — the largest remaining semantic risk surface, and why it must be left alone

- MECHANISM (census over all 40 cand_0003 traces): eight tasks print a worked-value disagreement
  and override the sheet in favour of their own rule. **All eight are correct**, so any new rule
  in this area can only flip a right answer wrong — which is why cand_0004 did not touch it.
  Grouped by the cause the agent invoked: stale formula cache (`48620` `'Yellow'`→`'Red'`);
  Excel error text in the pre-existing cell (`55049` 12 cells of `#VALUE!`→numbers, `56563`
  `#NUM!`→77772.6); placeholder text (`59595` `'n/a'`→4); an old formula the instruction says to
  modify (`6698` 6773→2592); a self-invented identity that was violated and rightly dismissed
  (`7902` `T4` worked value 1 vs its own `D4*L4` = 3.5999999999999996 — note the round still
  closed with "covered worked cells agree", a claim the printed evidence does not entitle).
- **The thinnest margin in the whole split is `9726`:** its single graded cell `J2` was pre-filled
  with `datetime(2016,5,14)` and the agent wrote `datetime(2016,6,12)`, justified **solely** by
  the instruction's own stated example, with no second corroborating signal. One cell, no margin.
  Any future edit that weakens "a stated example is authoritative" costs this task — as does any
  edit that strengthens "a pre-filled answer cell is ground truth" (cand_0001 already proved that
  direction costs `402-43`).
- Promising but not yet tried: nothing, until a *failing* example of this class exists. Without
  one, every available edit here is unverifiable by construction.

## When val saturates, the gate can no longer accept anything

- MECHANISM, arithmetic (confirmed by `rejected.jsonl`'s own formula):  …[+4014 chars truncated]

# META-INSIGHTS — about the optimization PROCESS itself (this run)

Not about the capability — about HOW this run is searching for it: which strategies/edit classes/algorithms are helping vs stalling, and what to try next iteration. Update at the end of the run at minimum; sooner if a plateau or a clear strategy shift is worth recording now. Structure each addition as:

    ## Iteration <id> (or 'run so far')
    - Strategy tried, and whether it moved val (cite LEDGER rows):
    - Plateau/stall signal, if any, and the lever switched to:
    - What to try next iteration:

## Iteration cand_0001
- Strategy tried, and whether it moved val: unknown at write time (no LEDGER row yet). The
  strategy was: cluster all 40 trajectories first, then **read the scorer and the adapter
  before writing a single word of prompt**. That was the highest-value move of the iteration —
  the whole dominant cluster is a property of `evaluation.compare_workbooks`
  (`data_only=True`, no recalc) that no amount of trace-reading alone would have stated
  precisely, and the exact type-normalisation table came straight out of `transform_value`.
  Recommend every future iteration on this benchmark re-read the scorer before proposing.
- Second useful move: **testing my own prompt artifacts** instead of trusting them. Two real
  defects were caught that way — (a) the adapter's `_task_template_error` rejected an
  f-string `{left}` in my verification snippet as an unknown placeholder, which would have
  scored EVERY task 0; (b) my first verification snippet asserted on a `data_only=True` read,
  where a leftover formula shows up as `None`, so the assertion could never fire — it needed a
  second `data_only=False` load. Both were invisible on inspection. Running
  `_task_template_error` + `str.format` + `compile()` on the rendered template costs seconds
  and should be mandatory whenever `task_template.md` is touched.
- Plateau/stall signal, if any: none yet (iteration 1 of 5).
- What to try next iteration: let the per-task RESULT decide the lever rather than guessing.
  If the ~15 "logic was already right" tasks flipped, the formula cluster is closed and the
  residual is logic/scope — switch from contract text to per-class worked examples and
  consider PRUNING prompt.md rather than extending it. If they did NOT flip, the contract was
  read and ignored, which means the lever must become structural (make the agent emit the
  verification output) rather than more prose.

## Iteration cand_0002
- Strategy tried, and whether it moved val: unknown at write time. The strategy was **read the
  parent's `broke={}` first and treat it as the primary signal, ahead of the failing-task list**.
  LEDGER row 1 (cand_0001 ACCEPT, `broke={402-43}`) turned out to explain *two* of the three
  residual failures: both `402-43` and `59595` are the parent's own highest-value edit
  over-applied. That reframed the iteration from "add fixes for 3 unrelated tasks" to "narrow one
  over-strong rule, then fix the genuine one-off". **Recommendation for any future iteration: a
  one-task `broke={}` on an ACCEPTED parent is not noise to be shrugged off because the parent
  won on net — it is a named, pre-diagnosed defect with a trace you can read, and it may be
  under-counted, since a rule stated too absolutely can also be suppressing tasks that were
  already failing for other reasons.**
- Second finding, and the one I would most want a future iteration to inherit: **audit BEFORE
  you ship, not after — and audit asymmetrically.** I wrote six edits, then ran a blast-radius
  audit over all 37 passing traces plus a pre-filled-cell census, and the audit changed **four of
  the six**. The worst was my own draft of the rule check: "if a pair disagrees, fix the rule"
  would have pushed ~10 passing tasks to break a *correct* rule to match a worked cell that is
  not evidence — a hand-rounded `0.1707` (`9569`), float noise `106.53999999999999` (`54144`),
  stale/`#VALUE!` formula caches (`6698`/`48620`/`55049`/`56563`), a neighbouring column computed
  by a different rule (`8942`/`37456`/`267-18`), and a prose/sheet case difference (`53383`).
  The asymmetry is the general law here: with 37 passing and 3 failing, **an edit that tells the
  agent to distrust its own computation is far more dangerous than one that tells it to distrust
  the sheet**, and it needs the benign-cause census attached before it ships. The census is also
  what caught `80-42` holding literal `'N/A'` as real data, which killed my first
  character-list-based placeholder rule and forced a re-derivation-based discriminator.
- Third: **do not trust subagent reports on load-bearing claims.** I fanned out four read-only
  subagents (one per failing trace + one auditor), which was the right call for coverage, but I
  re-derived the two facts my edits actually rest on myself from the benchmark's own workbooks —
  `43436`'s gold rule (recomputed both candidate rules from the raw XML; they differ in exactly
  the 5 cells the grader names, which pins the rule uniquely and excluded a rival hypothesis that
  differs in 9) and the pre-filled-cell census. Both re-derivations changed the edit. Note the
  method that made this possible with no openpyxl and no `pip` in the analysis sandbox: parse the
  `.xlsx` as a zip of XML with `xml.etree.ElementTree`, resolve sheets via
  `xl/_rels/workbook.xml.rels` and strings via `sharedStrings.xml`, and convert serials with
  `datetime(1899,12,30) + timedelta(days=n)`. Worth doing — the failing task's *gold rule* is
  recoverable from the grader's error signature far more often than it looks.
- Fourth, a cheap discipline: **count the round budget before adding a verification step.** 28 of
  37 passing tasks finish in 4 assistant turns and 8 in 5 — i.e. 8 tasks use all 3 of their
  `VERIFY_TURNS` with zero spare. So every new print this iteration went into the *existing*
  step-3 script in the same round. An edit that adds a round is a silent regression on those 8.
- Plateau/stall signal, if any, and the lever switched to: no plateau (one RESULT, +0.575) but the
  **headroom collapsed to 0.075 while one broken passing task costs 0.025**. The search is now
  regression-bound, not idea-bound, which inverts the instruction's "ship as many fixes as
  possible": the binding constraint is how many edits I can *prove* bounded, and the audit is the
  throughput limit. Hence the lever: spend the iteration's budget on the census/audit rather than
  on generating more candidate edits.
- What to try next iteration: let the RESULT pick the lever. (1) If `402-43`+`59595` flip, cluster
  1 is closed and only `43436`-class one-off logic remains — at that point the honest highest-value
  move may not be another prose edit at all but **robustness**: nobody has measured the 8 tasks
  that finish with zero spare verify rounds, and a single trial per task means a task passing at
  1.0 today is not proven stable. (2) If they do not flip, the discriminating condition was read
  and not applied, and the lever must go structural — force the agent to *print* the
  `existing value → my rule's value → decision` triple for every pre-filled answer cell, the way
  the rule check now forces the worked-value pairs. Restating a condition in prose a third time is
  the move to refuse. (3) Do not attempt the global "column header beats the instruction's prose"
  precedence rule without first building the prose/header conflict census across all 40 tasks; the
  audit found `59196` one pre-filled cell away from flipping on it.

## From cand_0003 (iteration 3 of 5, parent cand_0001 after cand_0002 was reverted)

- **The highest-value work in an iteration that follows a REJECT is not designing the next edit —
  it is attributing the last regression per task, from the broken tasks' own traces.** I fanned
  out four read-only subagents, one group per failing/broken task, and asked each for verbatim
  trace quotes plus a ranked attribution rather than a summary. The regression subagent produced
  the two-mechanism table that now opens PROCESS.md, and that table is what turned this iteration
  from "resubmit cand_0002 minus one bullet" into a redesign: the *direction* cand_0002 pushed was
  right (its `fixed={59595}` proves it) and only the **discriminator** was wrong (characters →
  type conflict). Without the attribution I would have thrown away a confirmed finding.
- **Gate arithmetic should be computed once and then drive ambition.** `rejected.jsonl` spells it
  out: `paired Δ̄=-0.0250 <= 0.2·SE=0.0087 (SE=0.0437, n=40, resolvable 2·SE=0.0873)`. So one task
  = 0.025 clears the bar at nearly 3×, while one regression cancels one fix exactly. **The target
  shape late in a run is +1/−0, not +3/−1.** This inverts the brief's "ship as many fixes as
  possible": the binding constraint is how many edits I can *prove* bounded, not how many I can
  think of. I still shipped six, but only because each one's blast radius was checkable against a
  census that already existed in INSIGHTS.md from iteration 2.
- **Audit the draft against the tasks it could break, before the draft is finished — it changed
  four of six edits this iteration.** Three catches worth generalising:
  (1) an *affirmative* branch is far more dangerous than a permission. My first type-conflict
  draft said "same kind of value → **leave the cell exactly as it is**", which would have
  regressed `6698` (stale numeric formula cache under an instruction to modify it). Deleting the
  branch and keeping only the narrow overwrite permission made the edit purely additive, so the
  passing behaviour it does not mention cannot change.
  (2) Phrase-family regression: a draft of mine read "never decide a cell's fate from its
  emptiness alone" — a paraphrase of the exact sentence that destroyed `80-42`. **Grep your own
  draft for the phrase family of every previously-regressing rule, not just the rule.**
  (3) Context cost is a regression vector, not a style issue. Any "one line per cell" print must
  be scoped to a set you can bound (`clashes` = pre-filled cells the rule covers) rather than to
  the answer range, because one task in this split has 47 975 of them.
- **Validate the template contract mechanically, every time, and do it before the handover files.**
  My step-2 draft wrote the dict as `mine = {coordinate: value}` in prose. `string.Formatter()`
  parses `{coordinate}` as a placeholder → `KeyError` inside `str.format` on **every task** →
  candidate scores 0. Caught only by replicating the adapter's own validation
  (`Formatter().parse` + `.format(**dummy)` + `compile()` on every python block). A prose edit can
  break the contract; a contract break is not a prose risk you can eyeball. Make this a reflex.
- **When the fix is a definition the agent lacks (KNOWLEDGE), prescribe and bound by grep.** For
  `43436` I wrote the section imperatively, stated its trigger as a *precondition* (per-record
  start date + end date + a cell labelled with a single moment), and then grepped all 40
  instructions for the moment/span lexicon to show the precondition is empty elsewhere (one
  lexical hit, `2768`, which has no dates). That grep is what makes a KNOWLEDGE section shippable
  rather than speculative, and it took minutes. Do it for every new section.
- Plateau/stall signal and the lever to switch to next: RESULTs are +0.575, −0.025 — not a
  plateau, but the headroom is 0.075 and two iterations remain. If this candidate flips 2 of 3,
  the remaining prose headroom is ~1 task and the honest next lever is **robustness, not more
  prose**: 8 passing tasks finish with zero spare `VERIFY_TURNS` and every task runs a single
  trial, so today's 1.0 is not evidence of stability, and nobody has measured it. If the candidate
  flips 0 of 3 with no regressions, the lever is to make the template's **write set derived from
  the computed set** (compute `mine`, then write from it) instead of stating the condition in
  prose a fourth time — restating a condition that was read and not applied is the move to refuse.

## Iteration cand_0004 (4 of 5) — the first iteration of this run that could not win, and what to do with one

- **Compute the gate arithmetic before choosing a strategy, not after.** cand_0003's own
  META note said to do this and it paid off immediately: parent at 1.000, no partial credit,
  bar `Δ̄ > 0.2·SE` ⇒ **Δ̄ ≤ 0 by construction, so no candidate can be accepted.** Five minutes of
  arithmetic reframed the whole iteration from "find more fixes" to "find the defects whose fix
  provably changes none of the 40 trajectories". That inverts the usual selection rule: normally
  you ask "might this help?", here you ask **"would this have changed any passing trajectory? if
  yes, drop it."** An optimizer that does not do this arithmetic will spend a saturated iteration
  shipping semantic edits with upside 0 and downside −0.025 per broken task.
- **A saturated val does not mean there is nothing wrong — it means the metric stopped being the
  place to look.** Reward is 1.0 on 40/40 and yet the capability ships a line of Python that
  **raises on 17.5% of tasks, deterministically**. The signal was in the traces' *exception
  stream*, which no reward number exposes. The generalisable move: when the focus block says "no
  actionable failures", stop reading scores and start counting (a) tracebacks, (b) assertions that
  fired, (c) round consumption against the real budget, (d) per-round output size. That census
  took one subagent and found the one thing in the run that is unambiguously broken.
- **Diagnose by correlating the failure against an input *feature*, not by reading traces one at a
  time.** The finding only became conclusive once I computed the set of tasks whose
  `answer_position` has no colon and compared it to the set of tasks with a traceback: identical,
  7 and 7, with no exceptions in either direction. A perfect two-way correlation turns "the agent
  sometimes crashes" into "this input shape always crashes", which is the difference between a
  guess and a fix. Build the feature census first; it is cheap and it is what makes the blast
  radius provable.
- **For a code-shaped prompt edit you can actually get a proof of boundedness — go and get it.**
  I re-implemented `range_boundaries`/`get_column_letter` locally (no openpyxl in the analysis
  sandbox) and asserted that the new `coords()` helper returns an element-identical list to the
  line it replaces on every multi-cell range in the split. That upgrades "I think this is safe" to
  "the 33 unaffected tasks see the same `cells` object". Prose edits can never be verified this
  way; **edits to code the prompt ships can**, which makes them the best value in a
  regression-bound regime. Prefer them when both are available.
- **Trust the subagent for coverage, re-derive for load-bearing claims — and note that it earned
  its keep on the two things I had missed.** I had the single-cell/traceback correlation myself;
  the subagent added (a) that 2 of the 7 crashes are in the agent's *own* round-1 code, not the
  template's line — without which the fix would have covered 5 of 7 and I would have believed it
  was 7 of 7 — and (b) that the context bomb is entirely a round-1 phenomenon (33 186 chars on
  `80-42`) while step 3's printing is already capped. Both changed the shipped diff. The pattern
  that works: ask for a *census with verbatim quotes and counts*, not a summary.
- **The adapter is capability documentation.** Three of the five edits rest on facts only readable
  there — `VERIFY_TURNS=3` with `verify_left -= 1` on any non-writing round (so a *raising* round
  costs a third of the verification budget), `MAX_TURNS=30` never binding, and
  `_task_template_error`'s exact validation. cand_0001's META note said "re-read the scorer before
  proposing"; extend it to the adapter's turn loop. Also: the fact that a *rewriting* round is free
  was deliberately **not** put in the prompt — knowing a fact does not mean stating it is safe.
- **Replicate the template validator with its compiled regex, do not retype the pattern.** My
  first validation run reported a bogus unknown placeholder `{placeholders}` purely because I
  omitted `re.DOTALL` from the comment-stripping regex and so left the file's own header comment
  in the text. Copy `_TEMPLATE_COMMENT_RE` verbatim. (The validation itself passed: 6/6 required
  placeholders, no unknowns, `str.format` OK, the rendered block compiles.)
- Plateau/stall signal and the lever: **not a plateau — a ceiling.** +0.575, −0.025, +0.075, then
  1.000. There is no prose lever left that a saturated metric can register. What the run should
  want next is not another edit but a *measurement*: at n=1 per task, `SE=0.0437` and the
  resolvable effect size is `2·SE ≈ 3.5 tasks`, so the run can no longer measure anything it is
  likely to change.
- What to try next iteration (the last): **do not go hunting for semantic edits.** If cand_0004 is
  rejected on a tie, that is the predicted outcome, not evidence its five items are wrong — read
  `PROCESS.md`'s equivalence proof before concluding anything. The genuinely valuable remaining
  move is to score the champion on the **test** split, where single-cell `answer_position` tasks
  (17.5% here) each burn a verify round under cand_0003. The one semantic cluster left — the eight
  `agree? False` overrides, all currently correct, `9726` resting on a single graded cell with no
  corroborating signal — is unverifiable until a failing example exists, and is a trap for an
  optimizer under pressure to ship something.

## From cand_0005 (final iteration of the run)

- **A saturated val split changes the optimizer's job, and the brief does not say so.** At val
  1.000 the gate can only return "rejected on a tie", so the expected-value calculus inverts: an
  edit cannot win a point, it can only lose one. The correct behaviour is not "ship nothing" and
  not "ship breadth anyway" — it is **"ship only edits provably inert on the passing
  trajectories"**, which in practice means edits to *code the prompt ships that demonstrably
  cannot run*, since those are the only ones whose blast radius you can prove rather than argue.
  This iteration found exactly one and shipped exactly one.
- **The breadth instruction is a liability at the ceiling, and that is now measured twice.** The
  two candidates that bundled speculative robustness edits cost −0.025 (cand_0002, 6 edits) and
  −0.050 (cand_0004, 6 edits); the two that shipped only what the traces proved were +0.575 and
  +0.075. Breadth is a *symptom* of a split with many failures, not a cause of improvement. Under
  pressure to ship something, the trap is the "I already have the file open" edit — cand_0005
  declined a genuine 1-line API fix (multi-part ranges) purely because no val task exercises it.
- **When a rejected parent bundled N edits, the recoverable question is per-edit, and it is
  answerable without re-running anything.** `broke={50768, 59595}` named tasks, not edits. Reading
  the two broken tasks' *current* traces and asking "which of the six edits could even reach this
  trajectory?" exonerated one edit (both tasks are multi-cell, so a single-cell guard is inert on
  them) and indicted another (both are small-range, so an inspection cap elides their answer rows).
  **Always do this before discarding a rejected batch wholesale** — one of cand_0004's six edits
  was a real, provable fix that would otherwise have been lost with it.
- **Strategies that stalled, cumulatively:** semantic rule-sharpening is exhausted on this split
  (the remaining 8 `agree? False` overrides and the `59196` header-vs-prose question are all
  *currently correct*, so no edit to them can be verified as anything but a risk — four iterations
  reached the same conclusion independently, which is itself the signal to stop re-deriving it).
- **What the search needed and could not get:** more *measurement*, not more propos …[+711 chars truncated]

# FRAMEWORK-IMPROVEMENTS — suggestions for cap-evolve itself (cross-run)

NOT about this capability or this run's result — about what cap-evolve the FRAMEWORK should change so FUTURE runs (any capability, any project) go better: a confusing prompt section, a missing tool, a file you wished existed, a gate that felt wrong. Optional most iterations; add an entry whenever something about the framework itself (not the task) got in your way or surprised you.

## From cand_0001 (spreadsheetbench, empty seed)
- The optimizer is told "you may not edit the harness/scorer", which I followed — but the
  single highest-leverage fact in this task (the grader uses `data_only=True` and never
  recalculates) is only discoverable by READING the scorer. It would be worth saying
  explicitly in INSTRUCTIONS.md that reading infrastructure to learn the contract is not only
  allowed but expected, and pointing at the scorer path. I spent several tool calls locating
  `third_party/spreadsheetbench/evaluation/evaluation.py` by filesystem search.
- There is no offline way for the optimizer to validate its own candidate. A tiny
  `scripts/validate_candidate.py` shipped in the working dir — run `_task_template_error`,
  `str.format` the template with dummy values, and `compile()` every fenced python block —
  would have caught both defects I found by hand, and an iteration that misses the first one
  (an unescaped brace) scores 0 on every task and burns a whole iteration of the run budget
  for a reason unrelated to the quality of its ideas.
- `prompt.md` existing-but-empty vs missing is a meaningful distinction in the adapter
  (`_read_system_prompt`) but is not mentioned in the "EMPTY SEED" section of INSTRUCTIONS.md;
  I had to read the adapter to be sure an empty file meant "no system message" rather than
  "fall back to the built-in default", which changes what the 0.350 baseline actually measures.

## From cand_0002 (spreadsheetbench, iteration 2/5)
- **Seconding cand_0001's `validate_candidate.py` request, with evidence that it is now a run-wide
  cost.** I rebuilt the same throwaway validator from scratch this iteration (placeholder contract
  + `str.format` + `compile()` every fenced python block in the *rendered* template) because there
  is still nowhere to put it: anything I leave in the candidate dir gets snapshotted with the
  candidate, and `/tmp` does not survive to the next iteration. Every future iteration that
  touches `task_template.md` will rebuild it again. A `scripts/` directory in the working dir that
  is explicitly **not** part of the candidate snapshot would fix both halves of this.
- **INSTRUCTIONS.md should tell the optimizer the per-task score granularity and the trial count.**
  Whether the remaining 0.075 is 3 all-or-nothing tasks or 40 partially-credited ones completely
  changes the risk calculus — with 37/3 and no partial credit, one broken passing task cancels one
  fixed failing task exactly, which is the single most important number for deciding how
  aggressive to be. I had to dig it out of `score.raw`/`trial_rewards` myself. One line
  ("each task is pass/fail, 1 trial, worth 0.025") would save every iteration that work.
- **The "ship as many fixes as possible" framing fights the gate once the capability is mostly
  working.** At 0.925 the binding constraint is not how many edits I can think of but how many I
  can *prove* bounded against the passing set, and the honest answer was "six, after an audit that
  changed four of them". The instruction reads as though timidity is the main failure mode; late in
  a run the main failure mode is an unaudited edit. Consider making the ambition line
  headroom-aware, or stating the brake with equal force ("an edit you cannot blast-radius is worth
  less than no edit").
- **`unresolved={}` in the RESULT stamp is well-designed and I want to flag it as working.** The
  parenthetical ("NOT evidence the edit touched those tasks; do not redesign on them") is exactly
  the kind of guard that stops an optimizer from chasing noise. More framework signals should carry
  their own interpretation like that.
- **Give the optimizer a read-only way to list the gold/expected values it is NOT allowed to
  encode.** I spent real effort reconstructing `43436`'s gold rule from the grader's error
  signature by parsing workbook XML by hand (no openpyxl, no `pip` in the analysis sandbox). That
  work is legitimate — it is how I verified the fix rather than guessing — but it is adjacent to
  the overfitting line, and an explicit sanctioned read-only "diagnose against gold, then write a
  rule that generalises" affordance (plus openpyxl actually installed in the proposer's sandbox)
  would make the boundary clearer and the work cheaper.

## From cand_0003

- **`prior_iterations/<id>/diff.patch` is truncated, and it truncated away the half I needed most.**
  cand_0002's copy ends mid-sentence at `... (truncated)` after three `prompt.md` hunks, so the
  **entire `task_template.md` side of the rejected batch is absent** — yet the rejected batch
  broke `80-42` partly through template-side verification printing. I had to reconstruct those
  hunks from the JOURNAL prose. A rejected candidate's diff is the single most informative artifact
  the framework hands forward; truncating it costs real iterations. Either raise the cap a lot, or
  truncate per-file (keeping every file's header and some hunks) rather than cutting the stream at
  a byte count, or drop `diff.patch` in favour of the prior candidate's full files, which compress
  far better than a patch and are what the next proposer actually diffs against.
- **The RESULT stamp names *which tasks* broke but not *which edit* the framework thinks broke
  them, and that attribution is re-derived from scratch every iteration.** I spent roughly half
  this iteration's budget on it (four subagents over the traces). If the harness kept the per-task
  trace of the rejected candidate alongside the accepted one — i.e. `prior_iterations/<id>/
  trajectories/<task>/` for the tasks in `broke={...}` only — the attribution would be a diff of
  two traces instead of an inference from one. That is a small artifact (2 tasks here) with a very
  high information ratio.
- **Nothing in the framework checks the template contract before scoring, so a prose edit can
  silently cost the whole candidate.** I caught `{coordinate}` in my own draft only by replicating
  `_task_template_error` myself. A pre-scoring dry-run that reports `MISSING/UNKNOWN placeholders`
  (and ideally `compile()`s the fenced python blocks) and *refuses the candidate before burning
  the eval* would turn a 0.000 into a free retry. The validation code already exists in the
  adapter; it just is not run at propose time.
- **Please state the gate arithmetic in INSTRUCTIONS.md, not only in `rejected.jsonl`'s reason
  string.** "paired Δ̄ must exceed 0.2·SE ≈ 0.0087, one task is worth 0.025, so +1/−0 clears the
  bar and +1/−1 does not" is the number that determines how aggressive every edit should be. It is
  currently discoverable only by reading a rejection you may not have.

## From cand_0004 (the first saturated iteration: val 1.000, 40/40)

- **When the parent's val is at the metric's ceiling, say so in the brief and change what is
  asked for.** The gate is `paired Δ̄ > 0.2·SE`; at 1.000 with no partial credit, `Δ̄ ≤ 0` by
  construction and `Δ̄ = 0` fails the bar — **no candidate can be accepted, whatever it contains.**
  Yet the brief still opened with "raise the eval score as much as you can", "ship AS MANY real
  fixes as you can", and "a timid one- or two-edit iteration is an under-used iteration". That
  pressure points an optimizer straight at speculative semantic edits whose upside is 0 and whose
  downside is −0.025 per broken task. The focus block *did* say "no actionable failures — seek a
  robustness/generalization gain", which is the right instruction; it is simply contradicted by
  ~40 lines of breadth-maximising text above it. Suggestion: detect `parent_val == max_reward`
  and swap in a saturated-mode brief whose success criterion is **"ship only changes that provably
  alter no passing trajectory, and prove it"** — plus an explicit statement that a tie-rejection is
  the expected outcome and not a mark against the candidate.
- **Surface the exception/traceback stream in the trajectory summary, not just reward.** This split
  reports 40/40 at 1.0 and *also* contains a line of capability-shipped Python that raises
  deterministically on 17.5% of tasks. Reward cannot show that; a per-task
  `tracebacks / asserts_fired / rounds_used / max_round_output` column would have shown it
  instantly. A cheap, high-value addition for any benchmark where the agent executes code.
- **Give the optimizer the real round budget, derived.** The brief and the template advertise
  `MAX_TURNS=30`, which never binds here; the binding constraint is `VERIFY_TURNS=3`, consumed by
  any round that does not change the output artifact — **including a round that raises.** The
  optimizer can only find this by reading the adapter's loop. Reporting "rounds used / budget, and
  which budget actually bound" per task would make round-cost regressions visible instead of
  silent.
- **Let a saturated run spend its remaining iterations on trials instead of edits.** At n=1 per
  task, `SE=0.0437`, so the resolvable effect size is `2·SE ≈ 3.5 tasks`: the run can no longer
  measure anything it is plausibly able to change, and `LEDGER.md`'s own `unresolved` column exists
  because of exactly this. An option to convert an iteration's budget into re-measurement of the
  champion (more trials, or an early test-split read) would be worth more than a fourth prompt
  edit, and would let the run distinguish "1.000 because the capability is good" from "1.000
  because n=1".
- **`git` is not usable for self-review in the candidate working dir.** `git status`/`git diff` in
  `work/cand_0004` report nothing (the dir is not part of the repo's worktree), so there is no
  built-in way to review one's own capability diff. I had to diff by hand against
  `run_suite/candidates/cand_0003/`. Dropping a `parent/` symlink (or a pre-computed
  `parent_diff.patch`) into the working dir would make self-review one command, and the brief does
  ask the optimizer to verify its own edits.

## From cand_0005 (final iteration)

- **Detect a saturated objective and change the brief.** The focus block said "No actionable
  failures in focus — seek a robustness/generalization gain", but the surrounding brief still
  demanded "AS MANY real fixes as you can" and warned that timidity wastes the iteration — while
  the gate, at val 1.000, can only answer "rejected on a tie". Those instructions pull in opposite
  directions and the measured cost of resolving them in favour of breadth is on the ledger twice
  (−0.025, −0.050). When parent val hits the ceiling, the brief should say so explicitly: *no edit
  can be accepted; ship only changes provably inert on the passing trajectories, or ship nothing
  and say why.* Better still, stop the run or reallocate the remaining budget to trials per task.
- **Surface non-scoring failures in the trajectory summary.** 7 of 40 traces (17.5%) crashed on a
  line of the prompt's own worked example, two of them losing an entire inspection round. The
  summary reports only reward, so this was invisible — it is found only by extracting traceback
  frames from the raw JSON. A per-task `rounds_used` / `exceptions_raised` / `recovered_from_error`
  column would have pointed straight at the single real defect in a saturated split, and would make
  "solid vs flaky" far more informative than reward alone.
- **When a rejected candidate bundled several edits, ask the optimizer to attribute per edit.**
  `broke={...}` names tasks. The instruction "keep the edits that did NOT appear in its broke={...}"
  is not directly executable, since edits and tasks are different types. A real, provable fix in
  cand_0004 was nearly lost with its batch; recovering it required reading the broken tasks' traces
  and asking which edits could even reach them. Either ask for a per-edit attribution table in
  PROCESS.md, or support one-edit-per-candidate / ablation candidates so attribution is measured
  rather than argued.
- **`history.jsonl` / `rejected.jsonl` were empty here**, while LEDGER.md and
  `prior_iterations/<id>/` had everything. The brief leans on `rejected.jsonl` as the
  already-refuted list ("read it and make each proposal STRUCTURALLY different"); if it can be
  empty mid-run, say that the per-iteration directories are the authoritative record.
- **Still true from cand_0004: no built-in way to review one's own capability diff.** This
  candidate's working directory is not inside the git worktree that tracks it (`git diff` returns
  nothing), so self-review means diffing by hand against
  `run_suite/candidates/<parent>/`. A `parent/` symlink or a pre-computed `parent_diff.patch` in
  the working dir would make the brief's own "verify your edits" step one command.
